newsitem.title: USA: Battered U.S. stocks may stumble if rates drift up.
newsitem.headline: Battered U.S. stocks may stumble if rates drift up.

text.p: Nervous Wall Street, battered by Thursday's sharp sell-off in U.S. stocks, will likely suffer further losses on Monday if investors see rising interest rates offering stiffer competition for equities.
While not predicting a major run for the exits, market analysts said stability in the bond market will be key to stocks finding their footing.
Major companies will not start reporting their first-quarter results for a couple of weeks, leaving stock investors little else to focus on than interest rates.
"If bond yields continue to drift up and we're still in an earnings vacuum, we'd probably suspect some rough times in the equity market," Douglas Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan.

Cliggott described himself as more sanguine about stocks' longer-term prospects, predicting the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks ending the year in a 810- to 850-point range. It closed Thursday at 773.88.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 140 points on Thursday, ending at 6,740.59. The blue-chip gauge recovered at the close after falling as much as 217 points in a late-session downdraft.
U.S. financial markets were closed Friday.

"I think Monday morning, if it gets ugly, we dip into the 6,550 area (on the Dow) and then bounce from there," Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. But he said such a pullback would not be "the end of the world" given Wall Street's sharp gains in the past two years.
Traders and analysts said Thursday's downturn was exacerbated by computer-driven sell programs after many market players had left for the holiday weekend.
But bargain hunters returning Monday and eyeing the bond market, may choose to wait on the sidelines.

Key to the pre-Easter selloff was the surge in the yield of the 30-year Treasury bond over the key 7 percent level. Robust economic data drove the long-bond yield to 7.09 percent Thursday, its highest closing level since 7.11 percent on Sept. 11, 1996.

The Federal Reserve raised its short-term federal funds rate last Tuesday for the first time in two years. Recent data has suggested the U.S. economy remains strong, convincing many on Wall Street that the Fed will be hiking rates further in order to ward off inflation.
Higher interest rates hurt stocks by offering a competitive return without the risks, and also by weighing on corporate profits through increased borrowing costs.
Also burdening stocks has been the strong dollar, which clips U.S. companies' foreign earnings.

"A lot of the market's leadership over the past 27 months has been negatively affected by either the strong currency or higher short-term rates," Cliggott said. "I think that's just another reason for thinking we're pretty much going to be stuck in a trading range for the foreseeable future."

Into the mix of heightened anxiety will come some critical economic data. On Tuesday the National Association of Purchasing Management's March survey is reported, followed by March employment data on Friday
Stock investors will also be on the lookout for any companies warning ahead of the earnings period that their quarterly profits will not match expectations.
"There's a lot to worry about," said Guy Truicko, equity portfolio manager at Unity Management Inc.
